were any visits missed or late.answer:
The database cannot determine missed or late visits. It only records completed visit start and end times, with no planned or scheduled times to compare against.

Evidence
- All recorded visits have status “Completed” in the schema.
- There is no scheduled visit table or planned start time field, so lateness and missed visits cannot be measured from this data.

What I couldn't determine:
- Whether any planned visits did not happen.
- Whether any completed visits started late.
- Whether visit duration matched the planned care time.
follow_ups: What are the planned visit times for each completed visit?
Do the visit notes for any completed visit mention delays or missed calls?
Is there a care plan for the service user showing expected visit times?

summarise alfred nkemelu s last 7 days.answer:
Alfred Nkemelu had 19 visits from 10 November 17:30 to 16 November 17:30. Most care was routine, but there were repeated signs of reduced intake, increased unsteadiness, a near-fall, and one episode of confusion or withdrawal.

Evidence
- Mobility: On 13 November he was “a little more unsteady” and used his frame throughout; on 15 November he had a slight near-fall while standing from a chair, with no injury and the office informed (visits 199, 205).
- Intake: He ate about half of breakfast on 11 November, initially declined fluids on 12 November, and on 16 November took only a small breakfast with fluids encouraged. The 16 November note says “poor intake again noted” (visits 193, 196, 208).
- Mood and cognition: On 14 November he appeared confused about his surroundings and needed reassurance. On 16 November he was “very withdrawn” with minimal engagement (visits 202, 208).
- Medication and continence: Medication was consistently recorded as taken or administered as prescribed, and continence care was completed across the week, with no medication issues recorded (visits 192, 210).
- Care plan fit: His care plan from 3 November already identifies dementia, frailty, poor intake, falls risk, unsteadiness and need for monitoring. The moving and handling assessment says one carer is usually sufficient, but a second should be used if he is particularly fatigued or unsteady. The near-fall and increased unsteadiness suggest this should be actively considered. These forms have no review date (forms 11, 12).

What I couldn't determine:
- Whether the near-fall led to any formal incident record, family update, or reassessment beyond “office was informed.”
- Whether Alfred’s reduced intake was measured over the full day or followed up clinically.
- Whether his increased withdrawal on 16 November continued after the last recorded visit.
